facts.statement: Infernogallus is classified as a caenagnathid theropod dinosaur.
facts.quote: A caenagnathid theropod.

facts.statement: The genus name of the animal is Infernogallus.
facts.quote: genus: Infernogallus

facts.statement: The only known species within the genus is Infernogallus jamesi.
facts.quote: species: jamesi

facts.statement: Infernogallus belongs to the family Caenagnathidae and is an oviraptorosaurian theropod.
facts.quote: Infernogallus () is an extinct genus of oviraptorosaurian theropod dinosaur in the family Caenagnathidae

facts.statement: The type locality for Infernogallus is the Hell Creek Formation.
facts.quote: Type locality: Hell Creek Formation

facts.statement: Fossils of Infernogallus have been found in the United States.
facts.quote: Country: United States

facts.statement: Fossils of Infernogallus have been discovered in the states of Montana, North Dakota, and South Dakota.
facts.quote: Region: Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota

facts.statement: The genus is known from multiple localities within the Hell Creek Formation in the United States.
facts.quote: known from multiple localities in the Late Cretaceous (Maastrichtian age) Hell Creek Formation of the United States

facts.statement: Five specimens of Infernogallus are currently known to science.
facts.quote: Five specimens are known, collected by different research groups at different times.

facts.statement: Infernogallus jamesi was formally described as a new genus and species in October 2026 by Gregory F. Funston and colleagues.
facts.quote: In October 2026, Gregory F. Funston and colleagues described Infernogallus jamesi as a new genus and species of caenagnathid theropod

facts.statement: The generic name Infernogallus is derived from the Latin words for 'Hell' and 'chicken'.
facts.quote: The generic name, Infernogallus, is derived from the Latin words īnfernus, referring to Hell, and gallus, meaning (male) chicken.

facts.statement: Infernogallus lived during the Late Cretaceous period, specifically the Maastrichtian age.
facts.quote: Age: Late Cretaceous (Maastrichtian)

facts.statement: The known fossil material includes a partial articulated skull and skeleton, along with several isolated cranial remains.
facts.quote: known from a partial articulated skull and skeleton and several isolated cranial remains.

facts.statement: Infernogallus is a small caenagnathid with an estimated body mass of approximately 12 kg.
facts.quote: With an estimated body mass of around 12 kg, it is a small caenagnathid.

facts.statement: The jaw muscle arrangement in Infernogallus may represent an adaptation for fruit eating, a trait unique among non-avian theropods.
facts.quote: It shows a reorganization of jaw muscles that may be an adaptation for fruit eating, similar to some modern parrots but unique among non-avian theropods.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen had an estimated body mass between 9 and 15 kg, based on a femur circumference and a femur length of 18.5 cm.
facts.quote: the holotype having an estimated body mass of between 9 - 15 kg based on the circumference of the femur, which is 18.5 cm long.

facts.statement: Histological analysis of the bones revealed growth marks indicative of an external fundamental system, signaling skeletal maturity.
facts.quote: histological analysis of the femur, fibula, and second metatarsal revealed a series of closely spaced growth marks near the outer surface of the bones, indicative of an external fundamental system (a signal of skeletal maturity).

facts.statement: Histological evidence suggests the animal was at least 6, likely 7, years old when it died, having reached full growth.
facts.quote: The histology further suggests the animal was at least 6—probably 7—years old when it died, at which point it was fully grown.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the reorganization of jaw muscles in Infernogallus was an adaptation for fruit eating.
facts.quote: It shows a reorganization of jaw muscles that may be an adaptation for fruit eating

facts.statement: Infernogallus had a large, circular eye hole that occupied almost 40% of the skull's total length.
facts.quote: The orbit (eye hole) is large and circular, taking up almost 40% of the skull's total length.

facts.statement: The infratemporal fenestra in Infernogallus was extremely small, measuring only 25% of the diameter of the orbit.
facts.quote: The infratemporal fenestra (a hole behind the orbit for jaw muscles) is extremely small, only 25% the diameter of the orbit.

facts.statement: The left and right mandibles of Infernogallus were fused and steeply upturned when viewed from the side.
facts.quote: The left and right mandibles (low jaws) are fused and steeply upturned when seen from the side.

facts.statement: The fused mandibles formed a toothless beak in Infernogallus, similar to those of living turtles and birds.
facts.quote: This forms the animal's toothless beak, similar to living turtles and birds.

facts.statement: A large groove over the mandibular symphysis in Infernogallus accommodated the maxillovomeral protrusion when the mouth was closed.
facts.quote: A large sulcus (groove) present over the mandibular symphysis (the point where the left and right mandibles meet), into which the maxillovomeral protrusion would have fit when the mouth was closed.

facts.statement: Infernogallus had a long neck consisting of twelve cervical vertebrae plus the atlas and axis.
facts.quote: Infernogallus has a long neck, composed of twelve cervical vertebrae in addition to the atlas and axis, the first two vertebrae that serve to attach the head.

facts.statement: The vertebrae of Infernogallus were hollow with extensive pneumatic air spaces.
facts.quote: The vertebrae are hollow, with extensive pneumatic air spaces.

facts.statement: Infernogallus had long hands capable of grasping.
facts.quote: The hands were long and would have been able to grasp.

facts.statement: As a caenagnathid, Infernogallus possessed long limbs and long, splayed toes ending in curved claws.
facts.quote: As a caenagnathid, Infernogallus has long limbs and long, splayed toes, with curved claws at their ends.

facts.statement: The 'elmisaurins' clade was recovered alongside 'caenagnathins' like Anzu, Caenagnathus, and Chirostenotes in a derived caenagnathid group named Eucaenagnathinae.
facts.quote: These 'elmisaurins' were recovered alongside several 'caenagnathins' (e.g., Anzu, Caenagnathus, and Chirostenotes) in a derived caenagnathid clade the authors called Eucaenagnathinae.

facts.statement: Researchers cautioned against formally establishing subclades like 'elmisaurins' and 'caenagnathins' due to instability and inconsistency in interrelationships, though they noted certain groupings persisted.
facts.quote: Due to the instability and inconsistency of interrelationships, Funston and colleagues cautioned against formally establishing these subclades, but recognized the persistence of certain groupings.

facts.statement: Infernogallus jamesi is a diminutive caenagnathid oviraptorosaur.
Infernogallus jamesi is known from a nearly complete, articulated skull that shows unique changes to adductor muscle organization.
Infernogallus processed soft food using anteroposterior mandible movement and ridges on opposing jaw elements.
Infernogallus likely had a specialized herbivorous diet consisting largely of fleshy angiosperm fruits.
It remains unclear what role caenagnathids like Infernogallus played in the Late Cretaceous proliferation of fruit.
Infernogallus had enlarged palate muscles and reduced temporal muscles, indicating a weaker bite force than other oviraptorosaurs.
facts.quote: The muscles associated with the palate are enlarged, while those associated with the temporal region are reduced, indicative of a weaker bite force than non-caenagnathid oviraptorosaurs

facts.statement: Infernogallus had highly textured jaw surfaces that allowed for crushing and shearing soft foods.
facts.quote: The occlusal surfaces of the jaws would have been highly textured in life, allowing for the effective crushing and shearing of soft foods

facts.statement: No gastroliths were found in Infernogallus, suggesting they were not used for digestion in this species.
facts.quote: The body cavity of Infernogallus is complete and articulated, including the complete gastral basket, but no gastroliths are evident, suggesting they were not involved in this species' digestion

facts.statement: Infernogallus was likely a frugivore that engaged in fruit defleshing similar to modern parrots.
facts.quote: Overall, Infernogallus was likely frugivorous, engaging in fruit defleshing, as in Pesquet's parrot

facts.statement: Caenagnathids like Infernogallus originated soon after the appearance of fleshy angiosperm fruits known as drupes.
facts.quote: Fossil evidence suggests caenagnathids originated soon after angiosperm fruits, including those with a single internal seed surrounded by a fleshy mesocarp (called drupes)
